monitored_text: Resources / Materials / Tungsten Metal: Definition, Composition, Properties, and Applications Tungsten Metal: Definition, Composition, Properties, and Applications Written by Kat de Naoum Updated by Greg Paulsen 10 min read Published January 19, 2024 Updated November 20, 2026 Expand your knowledge surrounding the hardest metal on earth and learn why it’s valuable Before the late 18th century, strong materials certainly existed, but we were in for a surprise when tungsten came onto the scene, overshadowing all other metals in this respect. As the heaviest known engineering metal, tungsten has earned the crown for strength, weight, and conductivity. Due to its desirable characteristics, we at Xometry and our customers have worked together to create custom parts from the material. When you’re on the market for a material that can put up with immense wear and tear and extreme temperatures, tungsten will rise to the challenge. If you’re interested in learning more about this metal, read on to get an understanding of what tungsten is made of, how it works across industries, and how it’s made. What is Tungsten? Tungsten is a metal, and you’ll find it on the Periodic Table of Elements, under the symbol W and atomic number 74. Originally called wolfram, tungsten got its new name later, derived from mashing the words for heavy stone in Swedish ( tung and sten ) into one, which is quite a fitting name. The first name was in honor of one of the ores tungsten is found in. Engineers and manufacturers love tungsten for its extremely high melting point, 3,422°C, and impressive tensile strength. Although you might be most familiar with tungsten’s block form, which is light to medium gray, in its purest form, it’s actually bright white. Is Tungsten the Same as Wolfram? Yes, tungsten and wolfram refer to the same chemical element. The terms are used interchangeably, with "tungsten" more common in modern usage and "wolfram" originating from its earlier discovery and historical nomenclature. What Is the Origin of Tungsten? Brothers Juan José and Fausto Elhuyar, two Spanish chemists, get the credit for discovering tungsten and making it a big name in chemistry and industry. Still, the origin story is slightly more convoluted as tungsten was actually being used hundreds of years before – in China. It was also discovered by a Swedish chemist and German miners, but it wasn’t until the Elhuyar brothers distilled it into its metallic form that it really became a big deal and prominent material. What Is Tungsten Made Of? The type of tungsten we know and work with isn’t just tungsten alone. When it hails from scheelite ores, it’s known as calcium tungstate, which has the formula (CaWO4). When you find it in wolframite ores, it’s considered iron-manganese tungstate (Fe,Mn)WO4. Molecular structure of tungsten How Is Tungsten Made? You won’t find a hunk of tungsten lying around out in the wild, as it needs to be heated and combined with other elements to become the form that’s used for industrial and manufacturing purposes. First, you need to get the tungsten out of the scheelite and wolframite ores it hides in, and this is done by gravity concentration and crushing, which separates the minerals from the element. Scheelite and wolframite ores will go through flotation, fine grinding, and even leaching, roasting, and high-tension separation to get tungsten out. If you’re in need of ammonium tungsten paratungstate, acid leaching and autoclave-soda processes are most common. Once you get as pure of a solution as you need or have processed the ores, the tungsten trioxide powder can be heated and turned into its pure metal form. What Is the Melting Point of Tungsten? Tungsten possesses the highest melting point among all pure metals, reaching 3,422 °C. This exceptional property is attributed to its strong metallic bonds. This makes tungsten a crucial material in applications requiring high-temperature stability, such as aerospace and industrial processes. What Is the Color of Tungsten? Tungsten is hard, brittle, and has a steel-gray color when it is raw. However, pure tungsten appears as a gleaming white metal. This color variability is what makes it useful in so many various industries. What Does a Tungsten Look Like? Tungsten is a shiny silvery-white metal. Historically, it was used in incandescent-light-bulb filaments. However, it is not energy efficient due to high heat production. What Are the Chemical Properties of Tungsten? In the table below, you’ll see the chemical properties of tungsten and its reactions. In the following table, you’ll learn the physical properties of tungsten, including its boiling point and its periodic table group. Physical Properties of Tungsten Is Tungsten the Hardest Metal on Earth? Yes, tungsten is the strongest natural metal with a tensile strength of 142,000 psi. However, it is brittle and prone to shattering upon impact, limiting its overall durability. So, while it's incredibly hard, its brittleness prevents it from being crowned the most durable or “strongest” metal for most (ambient-temperature) purposes. Can Tungsten Be Processed by Laser Cutting? Yes, tungsten can be processed by laser cutting. Laser cutting is effective for tungsten due to its high melting point and excellent absorption of laser energy, allowing precise and efficient material removal. Is Tungsten Magnetic? No, tungsten itself is not magnetic. It has a low susceptibility to magnetism. However, tungsten carbide, an alloy of tungsten and carbon, exhibits magnetic properties due to magnetically susceptible elements in the alloy. What Are the Applications of Tungsten? There are several ways we’ve taken tungsten and made it workable across industries, covering needs for rockets, oncology, fusion power, and beyond. Here are a few applications you should know about: 1. Electronics When you’re building circuits, you can use tungsten as the interconnecting material between integrated circuits. It’s lauded for its electrical conductivity and resilience, so it’s a great choice when you require a good signal transfer and smooth sailing with interconnected technologies. 2. Alloys Tungsten makes for a great mix-in ingredient when you’re making alloys. It’s often thrown in with refractory metals<dynamic-value> molybdenum, to boost their properties and create items such as turbine blades, rocket engine nozzles, and even darts. 3. Fusion Power This power source works by garnering enough heat from nuclear fusion reactions, and tungsten is an attractive candidate when it comes to assisting the reactors where this takes place. There are a few reasons why scientists and engineers herald tungsten for this purpose, including its high melting point, great thermal conductivity, and low reactivity under neutron irradiation. 4. Medical Applications The medical industry is one that has found many uses for tungsten. If you’re a doctor, you might find it in gamma radiography and oncology instruments. If you’re working with radioactive materials, tungsten materials can create great containers for holding them. In procedures, you may find a tungsten alloy in the form of a radiation-resistant syringe shield. 5. Nanowires Like with other electronics, tungsten is a suitable option if you need a material with good conductivity and optical properties. Tungsten can be spun into nanowires that are useful for sensors, electronics, optoelectronics, and energy storage. 6. Military Materials Tungsten has its place in the military, too, offering several uses when it comes to weaponry for defense. You might discover tungsten that’s used in tungsten-alloy bullets, shrapnel heads, and armor-piercing projectiles. 7. Chemical Applications You can whip tungsten into solutions and chemical compounds as well, which are found in many industries. The list is varied, and you can find pigments, paints, lubricants, and inks all made with tungsten. 8. Jewelry You’ll find another modern-day use for tungsten in the jewelry industry. Because it’s stronger than gold, silver, and even titanium, tungsten has proven to be a great material if you’re making rings and necklaces. For these reasons, you’ll also see it used in drill bits, too. 9. Welding Tungsten plays a vital role in tungsten inert gas (TIG) welding , as you can tell from the name alone. Tungsten is made into a non-consumable electrode that creates the electric arc you use to weld. This type of welding is perfect for you if you’re working on more fragile projects and need extra control. Due to this, electrical discharge machining (EDM) is a popular way to machine tungsten." Kurt Pokopac Solutions Engineer What Are the Advantages of Tungsten? There are several advantages to be aware of when you’re working with tungsten. High temperature stability: As far as pure metal goes, tungsten impresses by having the lowest coefficient of thermal expansion, so it will hardly expand when you expose it to extreme heat. High density and weight: Tungsten is used for racecar ballasts because its density is 1.7 times higher than lead's. Good blend of conductivity and inertness: Tungsten is ideal for use in environments with a lot of electricity or radiation because it won’t react in the same way other chemicals would while still remaining conductive. High corrosion resistance: You can use tungsten in industries and environments where it’ll be exposed to water, solvents, and acid without having to worry that it’ll corrode. Highest melting point: Amongst its fellow pure metals, you’ll find that tungsten has the highest melting point of all at a whopping 3,422° C. What Are the Disadvantages of Tungsten? Hard and brittle: There are many ways in which you can make the most of tungsten’s hardness, but with some applications, it’s too hard, brittle, and prone to shattering. One example is that if you have the wrong size tungsten wedding ring, it’s not possible to resize it. High density means heavy: Although it may come in handy for ballasts, you might find that tungsten is too heavy for other uses where weight reduction is an important factor. Frequently Asked Questions About Tungsten Metal Is Tungsten Expensive? Yes, tungsten can be expensive. The cost depends on raw material expenses and production complexity. Finished tungsten product prices vary widely, ranging from $25 to $2,500 per kilo. The majority falls within the $100–350 per kilo range, reflecting the influence of raw material costs and manufacturing processes. Is Tungsten Stronger Than Steel? Yes, tungsten is stronger than steel. With a tensile strength exceeding 600 MPa, tungsten is approximately three times stronger than steel. Is Tungsten a High-Quality Metal? Yes, tungsten is a high-quality metal. In its pure form, it boasts the highest melting point at 3,422 °C, the lowest vapor pressure above 1,650 °C, and exceptional tensile strength. These characteristics make tungsten a valuable material in various high-performance applications. Is Tungsten Metal Valuable? Yes, tungsten metal is valuable. Its scarcity, combined with exceptional properties such as high melting point and tensile strength, contribute to its significant economic importance and widespread use in various industries. What Is the Difference Between Tungsten and Titanium? Titanium is a hypoallergenic, lightweight, and corrosion-resistant metal. Tungsten, on the other hand, is denser and heavier than other metals, making it more resistant to scratches but also more prone to fracture. Often made of a tungsten and carbon combination, tungsten carbide alloy gives tungsten rings special qualities not found in titanium. What Is the Difference Between Tungsten and Stainless Steel? Tungsten steel excels in wear resistance and heat resistance but is more expensive. Stainless steel is magnetic, offers better oxidation resistance, and has higher ductility for shaping.
